title: 3-Bet Strategy for Canadian Online Poker Players in 2026
excerpt: Learning to 3-bet well is the fastest upgrade most Canadian poker players can make. Here is how to build ranges, size bets and handle the response.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Ask a competent online player what separates a break-even grinder from a winning one, and 3-betting comes up almost immediately. A 3-bet is simply the second raise in a betting round — someone opens, and you reraise. It sounds mechanical, but how often you do it, with what hands, from which seats and at what size shapes your entire win rate. Most Canadian players at low and mid stakes 3-bet far too rarely, and when they do, they do it with a range so transparent that observant opponents fold everything except the hands that beat them.

This guide breaks down 3-bet strategy for Canadian online poker players in practical terms: how to construct a range, how to size, and what to do when the reraise gets called or comes back at you.

Why 3-betting matters so much online

A 3-bet does three things at once. It builds a pot when you have the better hand, it takes the pot down immediately a meaningful percentage of the time, and it denies the original raiser the cheap, in-position flop they wanted. That third effect is underrated. Players who open wide from late position are relying on seeing flops cheaply against passive opposition. Reraise them consistently and their whole strategy stops working.

Online play amplifies this. Hands come faster, opponents rely more on default patterns, and the same players show up in your games repeatedly. A player who never 3-bets becomes readable within an hour. A player who 3-bets with a balanced range is difficult to play against for reasons opponents often cannot articulate.

Building a 3-betting range

The core idea is that your 3-betting range should contain both value hands and hands that benefit from folding equity. If you only reraise premiums, competent opponents fold everything but the hands that crush you. If you only reraise speculative hands, you have no way to get paid.

The value component

Against a standard opening range, hands like big pairs and strong broadway holdings are clear reraises. The specific cutoff depends on position: you can 3-bet a wider value range against a late-position opener than against an early-position one, because their opening range is weaker and yours does not need to be as strong to be ahead.

The bluffing component

The best 3-bet bluffs are not random weak hands. They are hands with blockers and playability — suited holdings containing an ace or a king, and suited connectors that flop well enough to continue when called. A suited ace makes it less likely your opponent holds a premium ace, which increases how often they fold, and it retains equity in the pots you do play.

  • Position is the first filter. 3-bet wider in position than out of it. Playing a bloated pot out of position with a marginal holding is how bankrolls disappear.
  • Opponent tendencies come second. Reraise the player who opens too many hands and folds too often; tighten right up against the player who never folds to a 3-bet.
  • Blockers matter more than raw strength for bluffs. A suited ace outperforms a slightly better offsuit hand as a reraise candidate.
  • Do not bluff-3-bet the calling station. Folding equity is the whole point, and against a player who never folds there is none.
  • Stack depth changes everything. Deep stacks favour playability; short stacks favour raw equity.

Sizing your 3-bets

The standard online approach is to reraise larger when out of position and smaller when in position. Out of position you want opponents to fold more often, because you will be playing the rest of the hand at a disadvantage. In position you can afford a smaller reraise, since your positional edge compensates for giving worse hands a better price.

The other adjustment is for callers already in the pot. If there is a caller between the opener and you, increase your sizing — you now need to price out two players rather than one, and the dead money in the middle justifies a larger bet.

What you must avoid is sizing that depends on your hand strength. Reraising larger with aces and smaller with a suited connector is the most common leak in low-stakes online poker, and attentive opponents will notice within a session. Pick a size for the situation and use it for your entire range.

Playing after the 3-bet

Reraising is the easy part. Most of the money is made or lost in what happens next.

When you get called, remember that you represented strength and the flop rarely changes that. Continuation betting on boards that favour your reraising range — high, disconnected cards — is generally profitable. Boards that favour the caller, particularly middling connected cards, deserve more caution and more checking, because those textures hit the hands that call reraises far harder than they hit yours.

When you face a 4-bet, the correct response is usually to fold most of your bluffing hands and continue with your strongest holdings. Players who 4-bet at low stakes are almost always doing it with a narrow, genuine range. Calling a 4-bet with a suited connector because you have already invested chips is a classic sunk-cost error.

Our broader online poker strategy guide covers preflop fundamentals in more detail, and the same range-construction logic applies whether you are playing cash games or tournaments.

Adjusting for the Canadian online landscape

Where you play affects how you should approach this. Ontario players sit in a segregated, regulated market with player pools drawn from the province, which means you will encounter regular opponents repeatedly and your tendencies get noticed faster. Balance matters more there than it does in a large, anonymous pool where you will rarely see the same player twice.

Table selection also feeds directly into 3-bet strategy. A table full of tight, competent regulars offers few profitable bluff-reraise spots. A table with two or three players opening half their hands and folding to pressure is where an aggressive 3-betting strategy prints money. Choosing the right table is often worth more than any technical adjustment. Putting it into practice

If your 3-betting frequency is currently very low, the fix is not to start reraising randomly. Pick one adjustment: add suited aces as reraise candidates when you are in position against a late-position opener. Play that adjustment for a few thousand hands and watch how opponents respond. Then add a second. Incremental, deliberate changes stick; wholesale strategy overhauls collapse under the first bad session.

The players who beat Canadian online games consistently are not the ones with the most exotic moves. They are the ones who reraise the right hands, from the right seats, against the right opponents, at a size that does not give anything away.
